court: New York Supreme Court, Trial Term, Sullivan County
holding_summary: Court held that a grantor's release of 'all claims, easements, privileges, and rights' under an agreement creating a mill pond released her right to fish and boat there, since those rights arose from the pond-creation agreement rather than as an incident of her ownership of the underlying soil. Plaintiff was therefore entitled to exclusive control of the pond, and defendants' fishing and removal of no-trespassing signs were unlawful.
notes: Water/easement dispute over a fishing pond; 'incident of ownership' language concerns riparian/fishing rights, not compensated occupancy of a dwelling.

court: County Court of New York, Oneida County
holding_summary: Court upheld revocation of a hotel keeper's liquor license after the licensee pled guilty to keeping a disorderly house, holding the excise board's summons was properly signed and that the board could take judicial notice that the disorderly conduct occurred on premises it had licensed. The decision turns on excise procedure and evidentiary sufficiency.
notes: Liquor-license revocation for keeping a disorderly (bawdy) house at a hotel; concerns excise procedure and vice regulation, not compensated short-term lodging as such.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term, First Department
holding_summary: Where a flat was hired 'at the rate of' $35 a month with no term specified, the court held the hiring defaulted to a yearly tenancy under the applicable statute absent proof of a definite term, and that the tenant's advance payment of a year's and later six months' rent negated any inference of a month-to-month tenancy. The court also addressed a district court's power to direct and set aside a verdict.
notes: Ordinary landlord-tenant dispute over the term of a full-flat residential lease between landlord and tenant; not a lodger/boarder arrangement or its regulation.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division, Fourth Department
holding_summary: Court held a town's 20-year-old suit to recover railroad stock it had transferred was barred by laches and was not a proper action to remove a cloud on title, and that the governing statute did not require the sale of the stock be made for cash. The 'incident of ownership' language concerned the power to dispose of personal property (stock).
notes: Municipal railroad-stock dispute; no relation to dwelling occupancy or lodging.

court: New York Supreme Court, General Term, First Department
holding_summary: Court held that a person who lives in New Jersey but conducts business in New York City 'sojourns' in New York for purposes of a statute governing where a witness may be subpoenaed under a deposition commission. The ruling construes 'sojourn' in a procedural/venue sense.
notes: Procedural deposition-venue case construing 'sojourner'; unrelated to compensated occupancy of a dwelling.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division, First Department
holding_summary: Court held that a tenant's holding over after expiration of a one-year dwelling-house lease creates, at the landlord's election, a new lease for another year regardless of prior notice of intent to vacate, and that this rule is not relaxed even where the holdover resulted from a family member's illness rather than the tenant's own convenience.
notes: Ordinary full-dwelling-house lease/holdover-tenancy dispute between landlord and tenant; not about short-term room letting or lodging-house regulation.

court: New York Supreme Court, General Term, Second Department
holding_summary: Court affirmed the validity of preferences in an assignment for the benefit of creditors, finding the debts owed to the assignor's wife and sister-in-law were bona fide loans and not fictitious. The trial finding recited, as background, that the wife had kept boarders under an arrangement with her husband whereby she retained the profits and he paid for his board.
notes: Passing factual reference to a wife 'keeping boarders' as background for a creditor-preference/assignment dispute; the court never adjudicates the legal character of the boarding arrangement itself, so treated as a passing mention under the coverage rule.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division, First Department
holding_summary: Majority held the city of New York holds absolute fee title to the tideway under its colonial charters, so an upland owner whose title derived from a post-charter grant had no compensable riparian rights when the city filled in the tideway to build a street; the dissent argued a pre-charter Harlem-patent grantee retained riparian rights requiring compensation.
notes: Waterfront/riparian-rights and land-reclamation dispute; 'incidents of ownership' language concerns tideway title, unrelated to dwelling occupancy.

court: New York Court of Common Pleas
holding_summary: Court held a landlord holding a chattel mortgage on a tenant's furniture did not satisfy the mortgage debt merely by taking possession of furniture the tenant had abandoned, and that excluding the landlord's testimony that he never used or profited from the property, and excluding evidence of its value, was reversible error. The dispute arose after the landlord let the flat to a new occupant for the remainder of the original tenant's term.
notes: Chattel-mortgage/conversion dispute; the subletting of the flat is incidental to the mortgage issue, not an adjudication of lodging or short-term letting law.

court: New York Court of Common Pleas, General Term
holding_summary: Court held a steamboat company liable, without proof of negligence, for money taken from a passenger's locked stateroom at night, applying to water carriers a liability analogous to an innkeeper's. The court declined to extend to steamboat companies the contrary rule for sleeping-car companies, which furnish lodging alone (not victuals and lodging) to a limited class of ticketed passengers and so are not treated as innkeepers.
notes: Carrier-liability case analogizing steamboats/sleeping-cars to innkeepers for lost-property purposes; discusses 'lodging' only as a doctrinal analogy for baggage liability, not compensated occupancy of a household dwelling or lodging-house regulation.

court: New York Superior Court, Equity Term
holding_summary: In a divorce action, the court found circumstantial evidence of adultery sufficient, including that the defendant and the co-respondent (who kept the flat where he boarded) were seen undressed and kissing, and had misrepresented their relationship as in-laws. The court remarked that their conduct exceeded ordinary relations between a 'boarding-house keeper and boarder.'
notes: Divorce/adultery case; the 'boarding-house keeper and boarder' reference is a passing rhetorical comparison, not a ruling on lodging law or its regulation.

court: New York Supreme Court, General Term, Fourth Department
holding_summary: Court reversed a defense verdict in a wrongful-death boat-collision case, holding it was error to admit testimony about a nonparty boat operator's general drinking habits, elicited in part through mention that he 'kept a boarding house' with a bar, where there was no evidence he was intoxicated on the night of the accident.
notes: Negligence/evidentiary case; boarding-house reference is incidental background used to introduce impeachment testimony about drinking habits, not adjudicated lodging-house law.

court: New York Supreme Court, Special Term, Ulster County
holding_summary: Court held a newly enacted certiorari-review statute for excise-license denials applied to a license refusal predating the statute's passage, and that an excise board could not refuse to consider an application on its merits merely because a majority of the board had campaigned on refusing licenses, absent an actual local-option vote prohibiting licensing.
notes: Liquor-license (hotel/innkeeper's license) refusal and excise-board procedure case; concerns liquor licensing, not lodging-house regulation or compensated dwelling occupancy.

holding_summary: Court held that money found on a customer-use desk inside a bank was not 'lost property' recoverable by the finder, because its location indicated it had been voluntarily placed there and merely forgotten by its owner, distinguishing cases (cited in passing, including one involving a hotel servant finding money left by a 'transient guest') where property found on a floor was genuinely lost.
notes: Lost-property/finders-law case; the hotel-transient-guest reference is a passing citation to another jurisdiction's case, not an adjudication involving lodging here.

court: County Court of New York, Rockland County
holding_summary: Court held that an agreement letting the defendant quarry stone on the plaintiff's land in exchange for one-fifth of sale proceeds, with no fixed term, created a tenancy at will removable by summary proceedings, since the arrangement was a landlord-tenant relationship (rent) rather than a joint-ownership share arrangement.
notes: Landlord-tenant dispute over commercial quarrying rights on land, not a dwelling or lodging arrangement.

court: New York Court of Common Pleas, General Term
holding_summary: Court held an oral assignment of rents to become due was void under the statute of frauds because rent is an incident of real-property ownership requiring a writing to assign, and that the defendant had constructive notice of a recorded deed transferring ownership and was estopped from claiming the disputed rents after accepting an agency from the new owner.
notes: Rent-assignment/statute-of-frauds dispute concerning ownership of rental income; unrelated to the character or regulation of lodging or short-term letting.

holding_summary: Court held that a tenant of commercial store premises could raise, as a defense to a rent claim, damages caused by the landlord's permitted interference with the tenant's beneficial use of the premises (removing a partition that forced patrons through a disreputable bar-room below), even absent a technical eviction, entitling the tenant to abandon the premises and defeat the rent claim.
notes: Commercial lease/constructive-eviction dispute over a store and offices; not a dwelling or lodging-house case.

holding_summary: Court upheld a gift mortis causa where the decedent, on the day of her death, delivered to her sister a receipt evidencing money held on deposit and declared she was giving her that money; delivery of the receipt sufficed since the sister already possessed the funds. The court also held a general objection to deposition testimony on 'mental capacity' too unspecific to preserve error.
notes: Gift mortis causa and testamentary-capacity case; the decedent's prior boarding-house keeping is background biography establishing the source of the money, not adjudicated lodging law.
